title: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 16 Startup Metrics
text:
## The 16 Startup Metrics (a16z)

One of the most-cited investor references for how founders and finance teams should define their core numbers. The point is discipline: many metrics are calculated inconsistently or gamed.

### Bookings vs. Revenue
Bookings is the value of a contract between the company and the customer. It is NOT revenue. Revenue is recognized when the service is actually delivered or ratably over the life of the subscription agreement. Letters of intent and verbal agreements are neither bookings nor revenue.

### ARR and MRR
ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue) should exclude one-time fees and professional service fees. ARR per customer should grow if you are upselling or cross-selling. A common error is to compute MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) by multiplying one month's bookings by 12, which wrongly includes non-recurring fees.

### Gross Profit
Gross profit includes all costs associated with the manufacturing, delivery, and support of a product or service. Total revenue alone is not enough: investors want to know how much of that revenue is actually profit.

### TCV vs. ACV
TCV (Total Contract Value) is the full value of the contract including one-time and professional-service charges. ACV (Annual Contract Value) is the value measured over a 12-month period; a growing ACV signals increasing value per customer.

### LTV (Lifetime Value)
LTV should be based on the NET PROFIT of the customer over the life of the relationship, not revenue and not just gross margin. Practically: revenue per customer minus variable costs gives contribution margin; average customer lifespan in months equals 1 divided by the monthly churn rate; LTV equals contribution margin times average lifespan. For early-stage companies, measure a conservative 12-month and 24-month LTV using historical data rather than projecting forever.

### GMV vs. Revenue (marketplaces)
GMV (Gross Merchandise Volume) is the total sales dollar volume transacting through the marketplace. Revenue is only the portion of GMV the marketplace takes (transaction fees, ads, sponsorships). Never present GMV as revenue.

### Deferred Revenue and Billings
Billings equals current-quarter revenue plus the change in deferred revenue. Billings is a better forward-looking health indicator than revenue alone, because a company can show growing revenue while billings (new business signed) are shrinking.

### CAC: Blended vs. Paid
Blended CAC equals total acquisition cost divided by ALL new customers across every channel. Paid CAC equals total acquisition cost divided by only the customers acquired through paid marketing. Paid CAC matters more than blended when assessing whether growth is profitable and scalable, because blended CAC hides the true cost of paid channels behind free/organic customers. Include all costs: referral fees, credits, and discounts.

### Churn
Monthly unit (logo) churn equals customers lost divided by prior-month total customers. Gross churn equals MRR lost divided by beginning-of-month MRR. Net revenue churn equals (MRR lost minus MRR from upsells) divided by beginning MRR. Net churn understates true losses by blending upsells with actual cancellations, so always show gross churn too.

### Burn Rate
Monthly cash burn equals (beginning-of-year cash minus end-of-year cash) divided by 12. Gross burn is total monthly cash outlay. Net burn is revenues minus gross burn and is the true measure of cash depletion and runway.

### Vanity metrics and chart tricks
Downloads, registered users, and cumulative charts are vanity metrics: cumulative charts always go up and to the right even when a business is shrinking. Watch for unlabeled Y-axes, exaggerated scales, and percentages shown without absolute numbers. Assess GMV/revenue/bookings first, then growth rate, then deeper metrics.

title: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 16 More Startup Metrics
text:
## 16 More Startup Metrics (a16z)

### ARR definition (strict)
ARR is recurring revenue on an annual basis. It should exclude one-time fees, professional service fees, and any variable usage fees. Only true recurring contracts count.

### ARPU / ARPA
Average Revenue Per User (or Per Account) equals total revenue divided by the number of users for a specific time period, typically a month, quarter, or year. As a benchmark example, Facebook generated $9.30 ARPU in FY2015Q2 from U.S./Canada users.

### Gross Margin
Gross margin equals total sales revenue minus cost of goods sold. Software companies typically run in the 80 to 90 percent range. E-commerce is far lower (Amazon was around 27 percent). Gross margin quality is why a dollar of SaaS revenue is worth more than a dollar of e-commerce revenue.

### Inventory Turns
Cost of goods sold for a period measured against the average inventory for that period.

### Viral Coefficient (k-value)
k equals the average number of invitations sent per user multiplied by the conversion rate of those invitations. Example: 750 new users from 1,000 starting users gives a k-value of 0.75. A k-value above 1 means true viral growth.

### Net Promoter Score (NPS)
NPS equals the percentage of Promoters (rating 9 to 10) minus the percentage of Detractors (rating 6 or below). Passives (7 to 8) are excluded.

The recurring theme across both a16z lists: define every metric precisely, separate recurring from one-time, separate cash from revenue, and never let a single up-and-to-the-right chart substitute for unit economics.

title: David Skok (forEntrepreneurs), SaaS Metrics 2.0, Detailed Definitions
text:
## SaaS Metrics 2.0: Definitions and Formulas (David Skok)

### CAC (Cost to Acquire a Customer)
CAC equals total Sales and Marketing expenses divided by the number of new customers acquired in that period. Include salaries, commissions, ad spend, tools, and overhead. Early-stage numbers can be misleading because a sales hire acquires few customers at first; measure CAC once the model is repeatable.

### LTV (Lifetime Value of a Customer)
Simple case (uniform ARPA, no expansion): LTV = ARPA / Monthly Churn Rate.
With gross margin (the correct version): LTV = (ARPA x Gross Margin %) / Monthly Churn Rate.
For accounts with expansion revenue, a fuller formula accounts for initial ARPA, monthly revenue growth per account, and the churn rate. Always use gross-margin-adjusted LTV, not raw revenue, or you will overstate LTV.

### LTV:CAC Ratio
Guideline for a successful SaaS business: LTV:CAC should be higher than 3. The 3x guideline assumes an 80 percent or higher gross margin. Below 1 you lose money on every customer; a very high ratio (say 5x or more) can mean you are UNDER-investing in growth and should spend more on sales and marketing.

### Months to Recover CAC (CAC Payback)
Months to recover CAC = CAC / (ARPA x Gross Margin %). Guideline: it should be less than 12 months. For enterprise land-and-expand models this is often longer, around 20 months, and can still be healthy if retention and expansion are strong. This metric matters most for capital efficiency because it tells you how long your cash is tied up per customer.

### Churn Rate
% Customer (logo) Churn = Churned Customers / Total Customers at period start.
% MRR (revenue) Churn = Lost recurring revenue from churn / Total recurring revenue.
Customer Lifetime = 1 / Churn Rate (in matching time periods). A 2.5 percent monthly churn implies a 40-month average customer lifetime.

### MRR / ARR
MRR is Monthly Recurring Revenue at the end of each month. ARR is the Annualized Run Rate = MRR x 12.

### Negative Churn (Net Negative Churn)
% Net MRR Churn = (MRR Churn - Expansion MRR) / Beginning MRR. This goes negative when expansion revenue from existing customers outstrips revenue lost to churn. Achieving negative net churn is described as a great goal for a SaaS company because revenue from the existing base grows even with zero new customers.

title: David Skok (forEntrepreneurs), SaaS Metrics 2.0, A Guide to Measuring and Improving What Matters
text:
## SaaS Metrics 2.0: Core Narrative (David Skok)

### The two central guidelines
1. LTV should be at least 3x CAC. The best SaaS businesses have an LTV:CAC ratio higher than 3, sometimes as high as 7 or 8.
2. You should recover the cost of acquiring a customer (CAC) in under 12 months. The strongest companies recover CAC in roughly 5 to 7 months; beyond 12 months profitability becomes anemic.

### The three pillars of a SaaS business
Acquiring customers, retaining customers, and monetizing customers. Retention comes first: if you cannot keep customers happy there is no point acquiring more, you are just filling a leaky bucket.

### The Cash Flow Trough
SaaS firms spend heavily up front to acquire a customer but recover the money slowly through recurring revenue. This creates the P&L and cash flow trough: early operating losses that paradoxically get DEEPER as growth accelerates, because every new customer costs cash today for revenue spread over future months. As NetSuite CFO Ron Gill notes, even with perfect execution an acceleration of growth is often accompanied by a squeeze on profitability and cash flow. After reaching profitability a company must re-enter the trough to fund the next wave of expansion, which is why growth-stage SaaS keeps raising capital.

### Unit economics: the core question
Can I make more profit from my customers than it costs me to acquire them? Answering it requires LTV (total profit from a customer over the relationship) and CAC (total sales and marketing spend per new customer). Get the unit economics right BEFORE pouring fuel on the fire, because scaling a broken model just loses money faster.

### Why churn is the silent killer
3 percent monthly churn feels harmless on 100 customers but on a million customers means losing 30,000 customers every month. High churn imposes a hard ceiling on scale no matter how efficient acquisition is. In a comparative model, moving from positive churn to 3 percent NEGATIVE monthly churn produced revenue of about $450k, more than 3x greater, with growth still increasing rather than flattening. Retention and expansion, not just acquisition, drive the long-run curve.

title: Bessemer Venture Partners (BVP Atlas), Scaling to $100 Million
text:
## Bessemer: Scaling to $100 Million (SaaS Benchmarks)

### Efficiency Score (Bessemer)
Efficiency Score = FCF margin as a % of ARR + ARR year-over-year growth rate. This is Bessemer's version of the Rule of 40. Targets by stage: about 70% at $25 to 50MM ARR, and about 50% at $100MM+ ARR as growth naturally decelerates. The average efficiency score for public cloud companies (BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud Index) is closer to 50%, anchored by high performers.

### Growth Rate Benchmarks (ARR, average / median)
$1 to 10MM: 200% / 165%. $10 to 25MM: 115% / 87%. $25 to 50MM: 95% / 77%. $50 to 100MM: 60% / 60%. $100MM+: 60% / 57%. Growth Endurance: private cloud companies retain about 70% of the prior year's growth rate; public companies about 80%.

### Net Revenue Retention (NRR) and Gross Retention
Net retention averages around 120% to 140% depending on stage (highest at the smallest scale). Gross retention benchmark is 85 to 90% across stages. Top-quartile NRR ranges from 125%+ up to 145%+ at the earliest stage.

### Gross Margin
Expected range for most companies is 65 to 70% across all stages; top quartile is 80%+.

### CAC Payback
Average about 15 months at $1 to 10MM ARR. Segment targets: SMB under 12 months, mid-market under 18 months, enterprise under 24 months. CLTV/CAC: invest when the ratio is 3x or higher; avoid when it is below 1x.

### Operating expense ratios at $100MM+ ARR (% of revenue)
R&D about 35%, Sales & Marketing about 50%, G&A about 20%.

### Cash Conversion Score (CCS)
CCS = ARR divided by total capital invested (minus cash on hand). Roughly 0.5x at $1 to 10MM ARR, rising to about 1.0x at $100MM+. Best-in-class is 1.0x or higher, meaning you generated a dollar of ARR for every dollar of capital consumed.

### Rule of 40
The Rule of 40: a company's growth rate plus profit margin should exceed 40%. Bessemer notes the BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud Index average is actually closer to 50%.

### Typical IPO-ready profile
LTM revenue growth about 65%, net retention about 120%, gross margin about 70%, R&D about 30% of revenue, S&M about 55%, G&A about 20%, FCF margin about -20%, with minimum GAAP LTM revenue of $100MM+ (the 2020/2021 cohort averaged $220MM).

title: David Sacks (Craft Ventures), The Burn Multiple
text:
## The Burn Multiple (David Sacks, Craft Ventures)

### Definition and formula
Burn Multiple = Net Burn / Net New ARR. It measures how much a startup burns to generate each incremental dollar of new annual recurring revenue. Sacks describes it as an annualized version of the Hype Ratio that puts the focus squarely on burn by evaluating it as a multiple of revenue growth.

### Benchmark table (venture-stage startups)
Amazing: burn multiple below 0.5x. Great: 0.5x to 1.0x. Good: 1.0x to 2.0x. Suboptimal: 2.0x to 3.0x. Bad: above 3.0x. A lower burn multiple is always better because it means less cash is consumed per dollar of new ARR.

### Relationship to other metrics
Hype Ratio = Total Capital Raised (or burned) / ARR. Bessemer's Efficiency Score = Net New ARR / Net Burn. Sacks notes Bessemer has the right idea but he prefers to flip the numerator and denominator so that a higher number is WORSE, which is more intuitive for a burn metric.

### Why he prefers it
The Burn Multiple is a catch-all metric: any serious problem will eventually show up in it. Weak gross margins, high churn, slow sales, poor pricing, or founder mismanagement all eventually flow through to burning more cash per dollar of new ARR. It forces founders to grow efficiently rather than buy growth with cash. In a downturn, investors weight the burn multiple heavily because it separates real, durable growth from growth that only exists because it was subsidized by the balance sheet.

title: Wall Street Prep, SaaS Magic Number, Formula and Calculator
text:
## SaaS Magic Number

### Formula
SaaS Magic Number = [(GAAP Revenue Current Quarter minus GAAP Revenue Previous Quarter) x 4] / Sales & Marketing Spend in the Previous Quarter. The x4 annualizes the quarterly revenue increase. An ARR-based version uses Net New ARR in the current quarter x 4 divided by prior-quarter S&M spend.

### What it measures
The efficiency at which a company's sales and marketing (S&M) spend generates incremental recurring revenue. It answers: for each dollar spent on sales and marketing, how much new revenue was earned? A magic number of 1.0 means the company recovers that quarter's S&M spend through incremental revenue generated over the following four quarters (a roughly 12-month CAC payback).

### Interpretation benchmarks
Below 0.75: inefficient. The current S&M spend may need adjustment, and pouring more money in will likely destroy value. 0.75 to 1.0: moderately efficient, healthy but with room to improve. Above 1.0: very efficient, a positive sign that the go-to-market motion is working and the company should consider investing MORE in sales and marketing to accelerate growth. A magic number above 1.0 is deemed a positive sign of efficiency; below 1.0 indicates spend may need adjustment. The lag structure (spend now, revenue over four future quarters) is why the metric is a proxy for CAC payback and sales efficiency.

title: Cobloom, The SaaS Quick Ratio (Mamoon Hamid metric)
text:
## SaaS Quick Ratio

### Formula
SaaS Quick Ratio = (New MRR + Expansion MRR) / (Churned MRR + Contraction MRR). It measures whether a business is gaining new revenue faster than it is losing existing revenue. Devised by Mamoon Hamid, co-founder of Social Capital.

### Benchmark
A Quick Ratio of 4 is considered optimal: the company adds $4 of new and expansion revenue for every $1 lost to churn and contraction. That level creates a steep, durable growth curve while minimizing the volatility associated with high churn.

### Worked example
To hit a 4.0 ratio with a typical 0.83% monthly churn, a company needs roughly 2.49% monthly growth: 4 = (2.49% + 0.83%) / 0.83%. As churn rises, the growth required to keep a 4.0 ratio accelerates dramatically: about 15% monthly growth is needed at 5% churn, and about 30% at 10% churn. High churn makes a healthy quick ratio nearly impossible to sustain.

### The critical warning
The quick ratio can mask unhealthy operations behind aggressive growth. $5,000 new MRR minus $4,000 churned MRR shows the same net growth as $1,000 new MRR with zero churn, yet the first scenario is far less sustainable because it is a leaky bucket being refilled at great cost. As a business matures, reducing churn becomes more important than accelerating growth. Always read the quick ratio alongside gross churn, not instead of it.

title: Wall Street Prep, The Rule of 40 (Brad Feld)
text:
## The Rule of 40

### Definition and formula
The Rule of 40 states that the combined value of a SaaS company's revenue growth rate and profit margin should exceed 40%. Formula: Rule of 40 (%) = Recurring Revenue Growth Rate (%) + EBITDA Margin (%). EBITDA margin is used specifically because most growth-stage companies are unprofitable or barely profitable under traditional GAAP metrics. Some practitioners substitute FCF margin for EBITDA margin; the principle is the same.

### Threshold and interpretation
At or above 40%: the company is likely in a favorable position to attain long-term growth and profitability. Below 40%: an imbalance that requires adjusting toward either growth or profitability. The rule captures the tradeoff between the two: a company growing 80% while burning (negative margin) can still pass, and so can a slow-growing but very profitable company. High-growth companies are allowed to be unprofitable; mature companies must convert growth into margin.

### Origin
Brad Feld popularized the framework in a 2015 blog post, responding alongside Fred Wilson to an investor heuristic used for software companies over $50 million in revenue. It became a quick heuristic for growth-equity and private-equity investors to balance growth against profitability.

### Applicability note
The Rule of 40 is most reliable for mature, established SaaS companies. It is unreliable for early-stage startups whose growth rates and margins are volatile, and it can be gamed at a single point in time, so investors look at it as a trend over multiple quarters.

title: ChartMogul, Net Revenue Retention (NRR)
text:
## Net Revenue Retention (NRR) and Gross Revenue Retention (GRR)

### NRR formula
NRR = MRR today from the group of paying customers you had one year ago, divided by the MRR from that same group of customers a year ago. It measures the revenue retained from an existing cohort after expansion, contraction, and churn over the period (usually 12 months). NRR is also called Net Dollar Retention (NDR).

### GRR
Gross Revenue Retention focuses only on churn and contraction within a cohort and EXCLUDES expansion revenue. Formula in words: (starting revenue minus churn minus contraction) / starting revenue. Because it ignores expansion, GRR can never exceed 100%; it is a ceiling that shows how much you keep before any upsell.

### Why the difference matters
NRR is always higher than GRR for the same cohort. NRR can exceed 100% because expansion (upsells, cross-sells, seat growth, upgrades) offsets churn and contraction; a value above 100% means the business grows revenue from its existing base even with zero new customers, the compounding engine of great SaaS. GRR isolates pure leakage, so a company with 130% NRR but 80% GRR is expanding a small set of accounts aggressively while quietly bleeding many others; both numbers must be read together.

### Benchmarks (top quartile by stage)
Early-stage: about 79%. $1 to 3M ARR: about 94% NRR. $3 to 15M ARR: about 99% NRR. $15 to 30M ARR: over 105% NRR. B2B SaaS companies should aim for over 100% NRR; 110% to 120% is strong and above 120% is best-in-class. Enterprise (ACV above $100K) should target 115%+, mid-market 105 to 110%, SMB at least 100%.

title: Corporate Finance Institute, The 3-Statement Model
text:
## The Three-Statement Model

A 3-statement model links a company's income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement into one dynamically connected model. It is the foundation on which DCF, LBO, and merger models are built. The three statements are not independent; a change in one flows through all three.

### How the statements link
Net income from the income statement flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet (equity), and it is also the starting line of the cash flow statement's operating section. Depreciation is an expense on the income statement (reducing net income), but it is a non-cash charge, so it is added back on the cash flow statement, and it reduces the PP&E asset value on the balance sheet. Interest expense on the income statement comes from the debt schedule that lives against the balance sheet. Changes in working capital (receivables, inventory, payables) forecast on the balance sheet drive cash flow from operations. Capital expenditure reduces cash (investing section) and increases PP&E on the balance sheet. Financing activities (debt draws/repayments, equity issuance) tie the debt and equity balances to cash flow. Finally, the ending cash balance from the cash flow statement becomes the cash line on the balance sheet, which is what makes the balance sheet balance.

### Construction order
Build the income statement down to EBIT, build supporting schedules (depreciation/PP&E, debt/interest, working capital based on days receivable, days payable, and inventory turns), then complete the income statement (interest, taxes, net income), then build the cash flow statement by linking to items already calculated, then plug ending cash into the balance sheet. If the balance sheet does not balance, a linkage is wrong. The model proves the accounting identity: Assets = Liabilities + Equity, and it exposes when a profitable company on the income statement is actually running out of cash.

title: Corporate Finance Institute, Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) Formula
text:
## Discounted Cash Flow (DCF)

### The formula
DCF value = the sum over all periods of CF / (1 + r)^n, where CF is the cash flow in the period, r is the discount rate, and n is the period number. For valuing a whole company, CF is typically unlevered free cash flow (free cash flow to the firm), and r is the firm's Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC). The core idea is the time value of money: a dollar received in the future is worth less than a dollar today, so every future cash flow is discounted back to present value.

### Terminal value (two methods)
Because you cannot forecast cash flows forever, a terminal value captures all value beyond the explicit forecast period (often 5 to 10 years), and it usually makes up the majority of the total DCF value. Method 1, Perpetual Growth (Gordon Growth): Terminal Value = FCF in the final forecast year x (1 + g) / (r minus g), where g is a modest perpetual growth rate below the long-run economy growth rate. Method 2, Exit Multiple: apply a market multiple (for example EV/EBITDA) to the final-year metric, assuming the business is sold.

### Enterprise vs equity value
Discounting unlevered free cash flows at WACC and adding the discounted terminal value gives Enterprise Value. To get Equity Value, subtract net debt (debt minus cash). A DCF is only as good as its assumptions: small changes in WACC or terminal growth swing the answer a lot, which is why analysts always run a sensitivity table on those two inputs.

title: Corporate Finance Institute, Driver-Based Planning in FP&A
text:
## Driver-Based Planning, Budgeting vs Forecasting

### Budgeting vs forecasting
A budget is a fixed financial plan for a defined period, usually a fiscal year: it sets targets that the business commits to and measures actuals against. A forecast is a rolling, continuously updated estimate of where the business is actually heading, based on real-time data and current trends. Budgeting is rigid and goal-driven; forecasting is dynamic and reality-driven. Mature FP&A teams run both: the budget as the accountability anchor, and a rolling forecast (often 12 to 18 months forward) that they revise every month or quarter.

### Driver-based planning
Instead of forecasting each line item off last year plus a percentage, driver-based planning builds the forecast from the underlying operational factors (drivers) that actually move the numbers. Revenue drivers: sales volume (units per product line or region), pricing (discounts, promotions, inflation adjustments), customer acquisition and retention rates, and market demand (seasonality, competitor activity). Cost drivers: supplier costs, labor efficiency, raw material expenses. Customer drivers: acquisition rate, churn rate, and lifetime value. Model the drivers, and the financial statements fall out of them, so when reality changes you change one assumption (say units sold) and the whole model updates.

### Building a driver-based framework
1. Define SMART business goals (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound). 2. Identify the key drivers that most influence financial outcomes. 3. Make explicit assumptions and track actuals against them, adjusting forecasts dynamically. Best practice: consolidate financial, operational, and market data into a single centralized source so every department forecasts off the same real-time numbers, eliminating conflicting versions of the truth.

title: Wall Street Prep, Contribution Margin
text:
## Contribution Margin

### Formulas
Contribution Margin = Revenue minus Variable Costs. Contribution Margin Ratio (%) = (Revenue minus Variable Costs) / Revenue. It is measured per unit or per product, unlike gross margin which is a consolidated view across all products.

### Variable vs fixed costs
Variable costs fluctuate with production or sales volume (inventory/COGS, direct labor, shipping, payment-processing fees, direct marketing tied to a unit). Fixed costs stay constant regardless of output (rent, insurance, salaried staff, equipment). Contribution margin strips out only the variable costs, so it shows how much each incremental sale contributes toward covering fixed costs and then profit.

### Contribution margin vs gross margin
Gross margin subtracts COGS (a mix of fixed and variable production costs) and gives a company-wide profitability view. Contribution margin subtracts ALL variable costs including fulfillment, transaction fees, and direct marketing, and it is computed at the product or unit level. This granularity is what makes contribution margin the right tool for pricing decisions and break-even analysis: break-even units = fixed costs / contribution margin per unit.

### Worked example
Price per unit $100.00, variable cost per unit $40.00. Contribution margin = $100.00 minus $40.00 = $60.00. CM ratio = $60.00 / $100.00 = 60%. Each dollar of revenue contributes $0.60 toward fixed costs and profit. This is the correct margin to use in true SaaS/e-commerce unit economics, not raw gross margin, because it captures the variable cost of actually serving and transacting with each customer.

title: Corporate Finance Institute, Working Capital Cycle
text:
## Working Capital and the Working Capital Cycle

### Working capital
Working Capital = Current Assets minus Current Liabilities. Current assets convert to cash within a year (cash, receivables, inventory, prepaid expenses); current liabilities are due within a year (payables, short-term debt, accrued expenses). It measures short-term liquidity, the cash available to run day-to-day operations.

### The working capital (cash conversion) cycle
Working Capital Cycle = Inventory Days + Receivable Days minus Payable Days. It is the number of days a business is out of pocket between paying suppliers and collecting from customers. Example: inventory days 85, receivable days 20, payable days 90, gives a cycle of 15 days, meaning the company funds operations for 15 days before cash comes back.

### Positive vs negative cycle
A positive cycle means you pay suppliers before customers pay you, so you must finance that gap (bank line, inventory financing, or receivables factoring). A negative cycle (for example inventory 85, receivable 0, payable 90 = -5 days) means you collect from customers BEFORE paying suppliers, effectively financing growth with other people's money, which is why grocery and marketplace businesses can scale on little capital.

### Why it matters: growing out of money
Rapid growth strains working capital. A profitable, fast-growing company can still run out of cash because every new sale ties up more cash in receivables and inventory before it is collected. This is the practical link between profit and cash: profit on the income statement does not equal cash in the bank, and a mismanaged working capital cycle can bankrupt a growing, profitable business.

title: ChartMogul, SaaS Metrics Refresher: Cohort Analysis
text:
## Cohort Analysis for SaaS

### What it is
A cohort analysis groups customers by the interval in which they started (for example, Signed up June 2021, Signed up July 2021) and then tracks a metric (retention, churn, revenue) for each group across every subsequent month of its life. Plotted as curves, it shows how each cohort evolves rather than collapsing everything into one blended number.

### The retention decay curve
SaaS retention is not a flat monthly rate. Churn is concentrated in the earliest months after signup and then flattens: subscribers are far more likely to cancel in months 1 to 3 than in months 9 to 12, and the longer someone stays, the less likely they are to leave. Modeling a single flat monthly churn rate therefore misstates lifetime value; a proper model uses the actual cohort decay curve.

### Why aggregate churn hides the truth
A blanket statement like 'our churn is up 2%' obscures where the problem is. Cohort analysis reveals, for example, that churn spikes specifically in month two or three, or that a particular signup month behaves worse, or that a product release or pricing change improved retention for cohorts that started after it. It lets you compare retention across plans, acquisition channels, or sales reps by segmenting the cohorts. The core lesson: retention improvements only show up in cohorts, and cohort curves, not a single averaged churn figure, are what you feed into LTV and revenue models.

title: Wall Street Prep, Cash Runway and Burn Rate
text:
## Cash Runway and Burn Rate

### Definitions
Cash runway is the implied amount of time a startup can keep operating at a loss before it depletes its cash on hand. Burn rate is the pace at which the company spends cash, usually stated monthly. Gross burn is total monthly cash expenses. Net burn is monthly cash expenses minus monthly cash revenue, the true monthly cash depletion.

### Formulas
Cash Runway = Cash on Hand / Net Burn Rate (in months). Monthly burn can also be derived as (beginning cash minus ending cash) / number of months in the period. Best practice is to average burn over 3, 6, or 12 months to smooth out seasonality and one-time items.

### Worked example
Cash on hand $200,000, monthly cash sales $50,000, monthly cash expenses $30,000. Net burn = $50,000 minus $30,000 = $20,000 per month. Runway = $200,000 / $20,000 = 10 months.

### Rule of thumb and levers
Seed and Series A companies are generally advised to hold 12 to 18 months of runway so they can hit milestones before needing to raise again. Founders extend runway by cutting costs, shutting underperforming units, raising prices, improving collections (shortening the working capital cycle), or raising capital. Runway is the single most important survival number: fundraising should start with roughly 6+ months of runway remaining, because raising takes time and you never want to negotiate from zero.

title: Corporate Finance Institute, Scenario Analysis vs Sensitivity Analysis
text:
## Scenario Analysis vs Sensitivity Analysis

### Definitions
Sensitivity analysis studies how the outcome of a decision changes when you vary just ONE input at a time, holding everything else constant (for example, how does valuation change as WACC moves from 8% to 12%, or how does profit change as churn moves from 2% to 4%). Scenario analysis changes MANY input variables together to describe a coherent future state.

### The three standard scenarios
Scenario analysis is usually built as at least three cases. Base case: current, commonly accepted assumptions, the most likely path. Best case: the most optimistic set of assumptions, the outcome if things go right. Worst case: the most pessimistic set, the downside if things go wrong. Together they bound the range of plausible outcomes.

### How they work together
Do scenario analysis first to establish base, best, and worst cases; then run sensitivity analysis within a case to see which single variable moves the answer the most. Sensitivity analysis isolates the biggest risk levers (a data table flexing one input); scenario analysis stress-tests the whole model against interconnected changes. Both let a finance analyst quantify risk and the range of potential benefits before committing capital, and they are essential companions to any single-point forecast, because a single base-case number without a range gives false precision.

title: SaaSCEO.com, Calculating LTV for SaaS: The Formula, the Math, and the Mistakes
text:
## Anti-Pattern: How SaaS LTV Gets Overstated

LTV is the single most-inflated metric in SaaS. The correct formula is LTV = (ARPA x Gross Margin %) / Monthly Churn Rate, or equivalently ARPA x Gross Margin % x average customer lifespan, where lifespan = 1 / monthly churn in months. Five ways teams overstate it:

### Mistake 1: Forgetting gross margin
Using ARPA / churn instead of (ARPA x Gross Margin) / churn. At 75% gross margin this overstates LTV by 33%; at 65% gross margin it inflates LTV by 54%. Never compute LTV on raw revenue.

### Mistake 2: Mishandling churn compounding
Churn compounds, it does not multiply. If monthly churn is 2%, annual churn is NOT 24%, it is 21.5%, because Annual Churn = 1 minus (1 minus Monthly Churn)^12. Examples: 2% monthly is 21.5% annual (not 24%), 5% monthly is 46.0% annual (not 60%), 10% monthly is 71.8% annual (not 120%).

### Mistake 3: Inflating the customer count
Counting trials, paused accounts, or free users as customers deflates churn and inflates LTV. Define a customer as an account paying recurring revenue at the measurement-period close.

### Mistake 4: Static one-time calculation
LTV is not a fixed property of the business; it changes month to month. Recalculate at least quarterly, ideally monthly.

### Mistake 5: Projecting long lifespans from thin data
Early-stage companies with a few months of history projecting a 5-year LTV are essentially guessing; with negative churn the naive formula gives an infinite LTV, so you must cap the horizon (12 or 24 months) and apply a discount rate for the time value of future revenue. Expansion-adjusted LTV can add upsell value but only cautiously.

title: Corporate Finance Institute, Bookings vs Billings vs Revenue in SaaS
text:
## Anti-Pattern: Confusing Bookings, Billings, and Revenue

The most credibility-destroying mistake in SaaS finance is reporting bookings or billings as revenue. They are three different things at three different times.

### The three definitions
Bookings: the total value of signed customer contracts, recorded at contract signing, regardless of when you invoice. It is a forward-looking commitment with no immediate cash or revenue impact. Billings: the amount you actually invoice customers in a period, per the contract's payment schedule; this is the direct cash inflow. Revenue (GAAP): recognized only as the service is delivered, spread over the life of the subscription, not when the contract is signed or invoiced.

### Deferred revenue
When a customer pays upfront, the cash collected but not yet earned sits on the balance sheet as deferred revenue, an obligation already funded but not yet delivered. It converts to recognized revenue over time as service is provided.

### Worked example (CloudSync)
A 3-year contract worth $300,000. Bookings at signing: $300,000. Annual billing: $100,000 invoiced upfront each year. Monthly GAAP revenue: $8,333, recognized evenly over 36 months.

### Why it matters
Celebrating a $120,000 annual contract as revenue the day it is signed, when accounting recognizes only $10,000 that month, misleads the board and breaks cash-flow projections. Bookings alone overstate growth if billing schedules stretch out; billings alone understate momentum if many contracts are signed but not yet invoiced. Critically, if you use bookings or billings instead of GAAP revenue in efficiency metrics like the magic number, you overstate sales efficiency and overspend on acquisition. ARR and MRR are normalized from active recurring subscriptions, not from billings, so confusing billings with MRR produces wildly inaccurate growth charts.

title: Phoenix Strategy Group, 5 CAC Calculation Errors to Avoid
text:
## Anti-Pattern: How CAC Gets Understated (Blended vs Fully-Loaded)

The correct metric is fully-loaded CAC = Total Acquisition Costs / Number of New Customers, where total acquisition costs include ALL sales and marketing salaries, commissions (fully burdened up front), tools, overhead, agency fees, content, and events, aligned to the sales-cycle timing. Five common errors that make CAC look artificially good:

### 1. Excluding indirect and overhead costs
Direct ad spend might imply a CAC of $2,000 when the true, fully-loaded CAC is $3,500 once you add salaries, office costs, and software. Most companies undercount CAC by 30 to 40% by leaving out headcount. Stripping costs out to flatter the number is the single most common founder error.

### 2. Confusing CAC with Cost Per Lead
CPL is only the cost to generate a lead; CAC is the full cost of turning that lead into a paying customer. A $500 CPL can become a $2,000+ CAC after conversion activities.

### 3. Timing-lag errors
January marketing spend that converts in March or April must be matched to those later customers, not to January. Ignoring the lag (common in B2B with multi-month cycles) distorts which channels look efficient.

### 4. Blended vs segmented CAC
Averaging a $50,000 enterprise CAC with a $500 self-serve SMB CAC hides the real economics and breaks LTV:CAC analysis per segment. Compute CAC per channel and per customer type, and rely on paid CAC (not blended) to judge whether growth scales profitably.

### 5. Overlooking one-time costs
A $50,000 rebranding campaign that helped land 200 customers is $250 per customer; excluding it understates CAC. The theme across all five: understated CAC makes the LTV:CAC ratio and payback period look healthy when the underlying economics may not be.

title: Wall Street Prep, CAC Payback Period
text:
## CAC Payback Period

### Definition and formula
The CAC Payback Period is the number of months a company needs to recoup the cost of acquiring a new customer. Formula: CAC Payback Period = Sales and Marketing Expense / (New MRR x Gross Margin %). Equivalently, per customer: CAC / (monthly revenue per customer x gross margin %).

### Why gross margin is in the denominator
You recover acquisition cost out of GROSS PROFIT, not top-line revenue. A customer paying $500 per month at 80% gross margin only repays $400 per month toward the cost of acquiring them. Leaving gross margin out understates the payback period and flatters unit economics. For SaaS, the relevant COGS are hosting (for example AWS), support, and onboarding.

### Worked example
S&M expense $5,600, 10 new customers, new MRR $500, gross margin 80%. CAC per customer = $5,600 / 10 = $560. Average MRR per customer = $500 / 10 = $50. CAC Payback = $560 / ($50 x 0.80) = 14 months.

### Benchmarks
Most viable SaaS startups target a CAC payback under 12 months. By segment: SMB roughly 8 to 12 months, mid-market 14 to 18 months, enterprise 18 to 24 months. Shorter payback means better liquidity, less capital tied up per customer, and lower insolvency risk; a long and rising payback period is an early warning that growth is being bought inefficiently. It is the operational cousin of the SaaS magic number: a magic number near 1.0 implies roughly a 12-month payback.
